Self-Hosting n8n on Hetzner: From Zero to Production

Gürkan Çanakçı
5 min read
·
1 day ago

--

You’ll find plenty of guides on running n8n locally with Docker. But that only gets it working on your own machine, and that’s not really enough. If you build an automation, I think it needs to be reachable from the outside world.

In this post, I’ll walk through how I set up n8n on my own server, why I picked this specific machine on Hetzner, and what I learned along the way.

Why Self-Host?

n8n’s cloud version is nice, but two things bothered me: execution limits and pricing that scales with usage. Between the bootcamp I mentor, my personal automations, and the dozens of workflows I like to experiment with, I wanted unlimited room to work. Self-hosting gets me that for a flat ~5 euros a month, no matter how many workflows or executions I run.

The only real cost is that you’re now responsible for managing the server yourself. That part wasn’t an issue for me though — I’m already comfortable with DevOps, so it wasn’t unfamiliar territory.

Choosing the Server: Why CX23?

Picking Hetzner was easy — it’s one of the best price-to-performance providers in Europe, and since I live in Germany, I also get a latency advantage.

In the console, I went with the CX23 plan:

  • 2 vCPU
  • 4 GB RAM
  • 40 GB local disk
  • 20 TB traffic
  • ~€4.75/month

A smaller plan (CX11 or CX22) would probably have been enough at first, but I already knew I’d want to add other containers next to n8n later — test instances, small services — so I left myself some room and went with CX23. 2 vCPU and 4 GB RAM run a single n8n instance comfortably; as the number of workflows grows I keep an eye on RAM usage, but so far it’s been smooth.

Three things I paid attention to on the server creation screen:

  1. Location — I picked the data center closest to me, for latency
  2. Image — plain Ubuntu, I wanted to build everything myself on top of it
  3. Backups — I turned on automatic backups, worth the extra ~€1/month

The Setup Journey

Once the server was up, it was time for the real work: n8n running in Docker, Nginx as a reverse proxy in front of it, and Let’s Encrypt handling SSL.

The flow, in short:

Internet → Nginx (80/443) → n8n container (localhost:5678)

I never exposed the container directly — it only binds to 127.0.0.1:5678, and all outside access goes through Nginx. That mattered both for security and for keeping SSL/domain management in one place. Here's exactly how I did it, step by step, in case you want to follow along and set up your own.

1. Prep Work

Connect to your server:

ssh root@SERVER_IP

Check the existing setup:

docker ps
ls /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
ss -tulpn | grep -E ':80|:443'

2. DNS

In your domain provider’s panel (Namecheap, GoDaddy, etc.), add an A Record:

Type Host Value TTL A Record n8n (or @) SERVER_IP Automatic

Wait 5–10 minutes, then check:

dig +short n8n.canakci.xyz

It should return your server’s IP.

3. Installing Docker & Compose

Remove any old docker-compose:

apt remove docker-compose -y

Add Docker’s official repo:

install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
chmod a+r /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc] https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(. /etc/os-release && echo $VERSION_CODENAME) stable" | tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null

Install and start it:

apt update
apt install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin -y
systemctl start docker
systemctl enable docker

Verify:

docker compose version

4. docker-compose.yml

mkdir -p ~/n8n && cd ~/n8n
nano docker-compose.yml
services:
  n8n:
    image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:5678:5678"
    environment:
      - N8N_HOST=n8n.canakci.xyz
      - N8N_PROTOCOL=https
      - N8N_WEBHOOK_TUNNEL_URL=https://n8n.canakci.xyz/
      - N8N_EDITOR_BASE_URL=https://n8n.canakci.xyz/
      - GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Europe/Berlin
      - N8N_SECURE_COOKIE=true
    volumes:
      - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n
    restart: unless-stopped
volumes:
  n8n_data:

The n8n_data volume holds all your workflows and settings — never delete it (more on why I care so much about this in a bit).

5. Starting the Container

docker compose up -d
docker compose ps
curl -I http://localhost:5678

6. Nginx Config

apt install nginx -y
nano /etc/nginx/sites-available/n8n.canakci.xyz
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name n8n.canakci.xyz;
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://localhost:5678;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}
ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/n8n.canakci.xyz /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
nginx -t
systemctl reload nginx

7. SSL (Certbot)

apt install certbot python3-certbot-nginx -y
certbot --nginx -d n8n.canakci.xyz

Enter your email, accept the terms, and choose 2 for redirect. Certbot updates your Nginx config automatically.

Verify auto-renewal:

certbot renew --dry-run

8. Test It

Open https://n8n.canakci.xyz in your browser and create your first admin account. That's it — your server is live.

What I Learned: Troubleshooting

The part that took the most time wasn’t Docker, as I expected — it was volume management. At one point I misconfigured the compose file and n8n ended up pointing at a brand-new, empty volume. For a moment, I genuinely thought I’d lost all my workflows. Turns out the old volume was still sitting there fine, compose was just pointing at the wrong one.

A few other issues I ran into along the way, and how I fixed them:

  • Port 80 already in use → run ss -tulpn | grep -E ':80|:443' to see what's holding it, then stop the conflicting service
  • Can’t get an SSL cert → make sure DNS has propagated (dig +short) and that port 80 is open in Hetzner's firewall
  • Webhooks/WebSockets not working → check that your Nginx config has proxy_http_version 1.1 and the Upgrade/Connection headers
  • Container stuck in a restart loop → docker compose logs n8n almost always points to a wrong environment variable
  • Rule: docker compose down -v deletes your data — never run it

After that scare, defining the volume as external: true and taking regular cron backups became my standard practice:

mkdir -p ~/backup
docker run --rm -v n8n_n8n_data:/data -v ~/backup:/backup alpine \
  tar czf /backup/n8n_data_$(date +%F).tar.gz /data

I run this every night at 3 AM via cron, and automatically delete backups older than 30 days.

Architecture Overview

Internet
   │
   ▼
[ Hetzner :80, :443 ]
   │
   ▼
[ Nginx (host) ]
   │
   └── n8n.canakci.xyz → 127.0.0.1:5678 → n8n container

The container is never exposed directly — everything goes through Nginx. Simple, single instance, easy to maintain.

What’s Running on It Now

This server is my automation hub now. It currently runs:

  • A LinkedIn job scraping + CV matching pipeline
  • Telegram-based lead capture bots
  • A RAG agent that tracks crypto prices
  • A bootcamp participant group-formation system

All of it lives under one n8n.canakci.xyz, managed from a single dashboard.

Who Should Try This?

If you’re running more than a few hundred executions a month and you’re somewhat comfortable with Docker and Linux, self-hosting is well worth it. The initial setup takes an evening, but after that you have unlimited room to play.

If you’re thinking about setting up your own n8n server and get stuck somewhere, feel free to ask in the comments.
